The question behind the work
Can a Rust rewrite keep what people rely on?

I’m testing real workflows against Redmine’s behavior while keeping its existing data. Speed and hosting savings still need a fair comparison.

Personal experiment · not yet for customer installations
Why I started

I love Redmine. I also want it to be faster.

Years of real work

I’ve been working with Ruby on Rails since 2005, and I still use it today. I’ve used Redmine since version 0.4.0, released on 2 January 2007. I like both. I use Redmine to manage real projects for myself and customers, so I know what a rewrite could lose if it gets the details wrong.

Performance is one reason I started RustMine. I’m rebuilding Redmine’s core in Rust to find out whether it can run faster and use fewer resources, while keeping the behavior and existing data people rely on.

This year, my hosting costs have almost doubled for the same service. I’m not paying for more resources. I’m paying more for what I already had.

Some of my customers have worked with me for over a decade. I built their Ruby on Rails applications over those years, and they are feeling the pressure of hosting costs too. I feel responsible for exploring whether I can help.

An experiment to measure

RustMine gives me a substantial project on which to measure what changes when the same work runs in a Rust implementation. I do not have those measurements yet, so I cannot promise lower costs or offer a migration path. I want to find out what the evidence supports.

How the work evolved

I wanted a feature-based rewrite from the beginning. We started with small experiments around Redmine’s tests, its database, and a few API calls. That gave us a way to check our work, but progress felt slow.

We then made the work items larger and more useful: not just reading an issue category, but completing a task such as creating an issue or copying a project. The tests stayed. What changed was what we asked the agents to build next.

RustMine is my private experiment, not a customer commission or a product I can offer today. I have not decided whether to release the source.

The promise I’m testing

Keep the data.
Change the application.

RustMine is designed to work with an existing Redmine core database. The goal is to keep your project history and data, without migrating them to a new system.

What I’ve checked so far

I compare specific tasks with Redmine 7.0.2 on SQLite, PostgreSQL, and MySQL.

  • The ruleLeave Redmine’s original tables and the record of changes to them alone. RustMine can add tables of its own.
  • TodayMany Redmine features still need work. I would not replace a live customer installation with this build. Plugins are outside the first version I’m aiming for.

How I check the work

Compare the feature.
Test the behavior.

Redmine is the reference. For each task we rebuild, I want to know what a person can do in Redmine and whether RustMine does the same thing.

01

Understand the task

Read the Redmine 7.0.2 code and try the task: what does the user see, who is allowed to do it, and what data changes?

02

Run Redmine’s tests

Use the relevant original Ruby tests to find details that a feature description might miss.

03

Try it in both apps

Give Redmine and RustMine matching sample data. Compare the pages, permissions, files, and saved results.

04

Review the result

Check the covered behavior, permissions, and saved data across the supported databases before I accept the change.

Features and architecture

Redmine gets a lot done through Rails. Its application code is only part of the implementation. Rails supplies capabilities that do not appear when you count Redmine’s own source lines.

With RustMine, I’m trying to reproduce the features and behavior people rely on, including how their data and permissions work. I’m not trying to reproduce Redmine’s Ruby and Rails architecture. Rebuilding Rails just to rebuild Redmine would miss the point.

RustMine has Rust dependencies too, and a different architecture changes where implementation code lives. That does not mean every additional line is justified. A raw application line count is a poor scorecard. Completeness needs tested workflows. Efficiency needs a fair measurement. Neither comes from counting lines.

Local preview · 18 October 2026

What already works.

These are usable paths in a local Rust build. Each is a bounded part of Redmine, not full parity or a customer-ready installation.

Projects and access

Sign in and manage projects, members, roles, settings, and supported project copies.

Issues and planning

Create and edit issues. Use queries, bulk actions, relations, and watchers, plus Calendar, Gantt, and roadmap views.

Time and reports

Log and review time, use project reports and saved filters, and import supported CSV files.

Team content

Use selected Wiki, Boards, News, Document, and attachment paths. Search and browse project activity.

Code and integrations

Browse selected Git and Subversion repositories and use covered API and webhook paths.

Still unfinished

Complex copy and permission cases, some Wiki, feed, and repository behavior, wider Redmine parity, the finished interface, and release readiness remain.

I have not measured a speed or hosting cost benefit, and this build is not for customer production.

Engineering journal

Eight recorded milestones.

How to read this: I put these entries together for the 18 October 2026 UTC snapshot from the work and tests recorded on each date. Dates shown use UTC.
Show
11 October 2026 UTC
Foundation

The first recorded RustMine code

The first commit included small Rust features, a list of Redmine tests, tools to compare both applications, and a check to protect Redmine’s original database tables.

Those checks gave us a way to test later work without losing sight of existing data.

12 October 2026 UTC
Browser workflow

Project work moved into the browser

We added browser forms for project work and recording time, so a person could complete those tasks on a page.

A page has labels, errors, and next steps that code-only checks can miss.

13 October 2026 UTC
Permission review

Search reached messages and code changes

We added searches for project messages and code changes, including checks for who is allowed to see each result.

Search should not become a shortcut around project permissions.

15 October 2026 UTC
Keeping data safe

Copying a project became a data test

We studied which content Redmine copies with a project and what happens if the copy fails partway through.

A half-copied project would leave people with a mess to untangle.

16 October 2026 UTC
Workflow rules

Issue forms began following Redmine’s rules

Some Issue fields must be filled in, while others cannot be edited at certain stages. We made the Rust forms enforce those rules.

A form should not save a change that Redmine would reject.

17 October 2026 UTC
Local preview

Draft previews and more repositories reached the preview

We fixed a profile link that sent visitors to sign-in, added draft previews in several editors, and made it possible to browse more than one Git or Subversion repository in a project.

People can check their text before saving and choose which repository history to browse.

18 October 2026 UTC
Local preview

Project membership and authentication reached the preview

A project manager can search for users and groups, add several with roles, change or remove members, and export the Members list as CSV. Administrators can set sign-in, registration, password, two-factor and session options in the Authentication tab.

That preview checkpoint passed 417/417 selected checks. These are tested local workflows, not full Redmine compatibility or customer production.

18 October 2026 UTC
Local preview

Email notifications and Issue settings reached the preview

Administrators can set a mail sender, choose notification events, adjust text and plain-text delivery, and send a test email. The Issues tab saves selected defaults for dates, progress, columns and public global queries; checked Issue creation and list/CSV paths use them.

The current local release passed 421/421 selected checks. Some downstream settings behavior remains unverified, and there is no customer production deployment.

No entries in this category.

After the first portMy plan

Then I have to maintain it.

Redmine will keep changing. If this rewrite works, RustMine will need to follow those changes deliberately.

  1. Follow Redmine releases and security notices. Work that has not shipped can be a clue, but it is not a change to copy yet.
  2. For each release, find the changes users will notice and check whether they affect permissions, files, or saved data.
  3. Add tests for those changes, then update RustMine’s behavior where needed.
  4. Review the result, test it with the supported databases, and check existing data before making a RustMine release.

Watch regularly. Ship deliberately.

I would review security fixes quickly, but a new Redmine change should not automatically change RustMine. Surprise software updates are rarely anyone’s favorite kind of surprise.

The resource question

Less hosting cost?
Prove it first.

I want to know whether RustMine can handle the same work faster or with less memory. That might reduce hosting cost, but I have not run a fair comparison yet. I cannot claim a speedup or savings.

How I would compare them
  • Give Redmine and RustMine the same data and the same everyday tasks.
  • Run them on comparable computers and expect the same quality of service.
  • Measure response time, how much work they handle, memory use, and hosting cost.

Choosing a faster language starts the experiment. It does not finish it.

Tools behind the work

What I use to build it.

For this experiment, I use Codex and a dedicated Mac mini. I keep the engineering decisions and review in my own hands.

Codex subscription

$200 monthly plan

I use OpenAI’s $200 monthly plan for RustMine and my other projects. That is the subscription price, not a cost dedicated to RustMine.

Dedicated hardware

Mac mini

I bought a 16 GB / 512 GB Mac mini for the experiment.

One reason I started RustMine was to try OpenAI’s GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6.1 Sol on an application I know well, using Codex straight out of the box without a custom configuration.

My job remains to understand the work, review its evidence, and decide what belongs in the product. I have not calculated the total cost of this experiment.
